title: Which email was it?
summary: Three reported emails, one real attack: read the headers, search the mail and proxy logs, find who clicked, contain it and prove how it got through.
simplification: Simplified simulation: headers are trimmed to the ones an analyst reads, and the logs to the lines that matter. Log lines follow Ubuntu 22.04's Postfix, Dovecot 2.3, OpenDKIM, OpenDMARC and policyd-spf formats, and Squid's native access log sent to syslog; every server keeps UTC. doveadm's column spacing is approximate. Domains use the reserved .example name (so the whois record is illustrative: .example names can't really be registered) and IP addresses are documentation ranges.

send.name: Email sent (SMTP)
send.say: From: Ashby Lane IT <it-support@ashby1ane.example>. Your mailbox password expires today.
send.explain: The attacker's server hands the email to Ashby Lane's mail server, like any other sender. It goes to three people at once.

fields.name: From (shown)
fields.explain: What the reader sees. The name is anything the sender types; only the address after it is checked, and this one is ashby1ane, with a 1.

fields.name: Subject
fields.value: Action required: your mailbox password expires today
fields.explain: Urgency and a deadline: classic pressure to act before thinking.

fields.name: Recipients
fields.explain: One message, three mailboxes. Postfix logs this as nrcpt=3.

fields.name: Sending server
fields.explain: The attacker's own server. The Received header records this name and address.

fields.name: Envelope sender
fields.explain: The MAIL FROM address in the SMTP conversation. SPF checks this domain.

spf_ask.name: SPF lookup (DNS)
spf_ask.say: TXT ashby1ane.example? Which servers may send its mail?
spf_ask.explain: SPF: the receiving server asks the sender's domain, through DNS, which addresses may send its email. The attacker registered ashby1ane.example, so they run its DNS and write that answer.

fields.name: Question
fields.explain: SPF only proves the server is allowed by the domain it claims. It says nothing about whether the domain is trustworthy.

fields.name: DNS query
fields.explain: SPF records are TXT records starting v=spf1.

fields.name: Also checked
fields.explain: DKIM checks a signature against a public key in the domain's DNS; DMARC checks the From domain matches what SPF or DKIM proved.

spf_reply.name: SPF record
spf_reply.explain: The record says 203.0.113.77 may send for ashby1ane.example, and that's the address the email came from. SPF passes, and so do DKIM and DMARC: the attacker set up all three for their own domain.

fields.name: Result
fields.explain: Passing proves the email really came from ashby1ane.example. It doesn't prove ashby1ane.example is who it claims to be.

fields.name: SPF record
fields.explain: Only 203.0.113.77 may send; -all means fail everything else.

fields.name: Logged as
fields.explain: The DMARC check's log line on mail01.

deliver.name: Delivered to the inbox
deliver.say: New message: Action required: your mailbox password expires today
deliver.explain: Every check passed, so the email lands in the inbox, not Junk. Priya's mail app fetches it over IMAP.

fields.name: Folder
fields.explain: The filter had no reason to doubt it: the domain is new, not known to be bad, and it passed every check.

fields.name: Link text
fields.explain: What the link says.

fields.name: Link goes to
fields.explain: Where it really goes. Hovering over a link (or long-pressing on a phone) shows this before you click.

click.name: Link clicked (HTTPS)
click.explain: Priya clicks. Her browser asks the web proxy to open a tunnel to the fake site. HTTPS is encrypted, so the proxy sees only the site's name and port, not the page or anything typed into it.

fields.name: Site
fields.explain: A copy of the firm's webmail sign-in page, on the attacker's server.

fields.name: Padlock?
fields.explain: The attacker got a certificate for their own domain. A padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.

fields.name: Proxy sees
fields.explain: Squid logs the tunnel as TCP_TUNNEL/200 when it closes, with how long it was open.

creds.name: Password typed in
creds.explain: Priya types her email and password. The fake page saves them, says 'wrong password' and sends her on to the real webmail, so nothing seems odd.

fields.name: Sent to
fields.explain: The attacker now has her password.

fields.name: What Priya saw
fields.explain: A common trick: the second attempt works, so the victim shrugs it off.

fields.name: In the proxy log
fields.explain: The form travels inside the encrypted tunnel. The only trace is the tunnel itself.

login.name: Attacker signs in (IMAP)
login.explain: Twelve minutes later the attacker signs in to Priya's mailbox with her real password. The server can't tell them apart: the password is right.

fields.name: Account
fields.explain: Now the attacker can read her email and send as her, to clients or to colleagues.

fields.name: From
fields.explain: Outside the firm: the same address that sent the email.

fields.name: Logged as
fields.explain: Dovecot's sign-in line. rip is the remote IP, the address that signed in.

findings.finding: The fake IT email went to 3 mailboxes (nrcpt=3): accounts, owen.reed and priya.shah.
Only Priya's laptop (10.0.5.41) opened login.ashby1ane.example, for 74 seconds from 09:27. Then it went to the real webmail.
At 09:41 priya.shah signed in to mail01 from 203.0.113.77, the address that sent the fake email: the attacker is using her password.
Sieve filed the 'Daniel Ashby' email in Mel's Junk folder: the filters caught it.
Harlow Print's email passed DMARC (opendmarc: harlowprint.example pass).

guided.label: Guided
guided.intro: Follow one phishing email from the attacker's server to a stolen password, and see why every check let it through.
guided.debrief: You've followed a phish end to end: a lookalike domain that passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC, a link that says one thing and goes to another, and a password used twelve minutes later. Next, predict each step in Practice mode.

practice.label: Practice
practice.intro: Same email, but predict what happens before each step.

spf_reply.q: mail01 asks ashby1ane.example's DNS which servers may send its mail. What will the SPF check say?
options: Fail: it's pretending to be Ashby Lane
Pass: the attacker owns that domain and listed their own server
Softfail: new domains always softfail
No result: SPF only works for big companies
spf_reply.why: SPF checks the domain the email says it's from, and ashby1ane.example really did send it. The attacker controls that domain's DNS, so it passes. Checks catch forgeries, not lookalikes.

deliver.q: Every check passed. Where does the email land?
options: Junk, because the domain is new
Rejected at the server
The inbox
Held for an administrator
deliver.why: Nothing failed, so it goes to the inbox. Some filters score brand-new domains as risky, but that isn't guaranteed, which is why people are the last line of defence.

creds.q: Priya is on the fake page and types her password. What can the web proxy see?
options: Her password, in plain text
The site's name and how long the connection lasted, but not what she typed
Nothing at all
The whole page as she saw it
creds.why: HTTPS is encrypted between her browser and the site. The proxy only opened a tunnel (CONNECT login.ashby1ane.example:443), so its log shows the name, time and bytes, never the password.

login.q: The attacker has Priya's password. What do they most likely do next?
options: Sign in to her mailbox
Nothing: passwords expire anyway
Send her a thank-you email
Attack the web proxy
login.why: A mailbox is valuable: client conversations, invoices to alter, and a trusted account to phish colleagues from. That's why speed matters once someone reports typing a password.

practice.debrief: You can predict how a lookalike phish gets through and what it leaves behind. Now investigate one in Challenge mode.

challenge.label: Challenge
challenge.intro: It's 09:52. Three people have reported emails this morning. Inspect each one, search the mail and proxy logs, contain whatever is real, then prove how it happened.

opening.say: I clicked the IT password link and typed my password. It said wrong password, then opened normal webmail. Is that bad?
opening.log: Start: Tom, Mel and Priya have each reported an email. Priya thinks she typed her password into something. Which email was it, and what happened next?

hints: Open each reported email. Compare who it says it's from with the real address, and check where its links really go.
One email passed every check. Read its domain letter by letter. Then search the logs for that domain to see who else got it and who visited it.
Search the log for the attacker's address, 203.0.113.77. Did anything sign in from there? Run doveadm who.
Contain it: remove the email from every mailbox, block the domain, reset Priya's password, then end her sessions. Order matters: ending sessions before the reset lets the attacker straight back in.

rootCause.q: Priya's mailbox is contained. How did the attacker get in?
options: Ashby Lane's mail server was hacked and sent the email itself
A lookalike domain the attacker owns passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and Priya typed her password into its fake sign-in page
The 'Daniel Ashby' email got past the spam filter
Malware on Priya's laptop stole her password
rootCause.why: The email came from ashby1ane.example, which the attacker registered and set up properly, so every check passed. Its link went to a copy of the sign-in page, the proxy shows only Priya opened it, and fourteen minutes later her account signed in from the attacker's address. Nothing was hacked: a password was handed over.
rootCause.evidenceQ: Which findings support that diagnosis? Tick the evidence, leave out what isn't.

evidence.text: Headers: the 'password expires' email is from ashby1ane.example, a lookalike of ashbylane.example
evidence.why: The heart of it: a domain one character away from the firm's, which a busy reader takes as the real thing.

evidence.text: Proxy log: only Priya's laptop opened login.ashby1ane.example, at 09:27
evidence.why: Shows she reached the fake sign-in page, and that nobody else did, so only her password is at risk.

evidence.text: Mail log: priya.shah signed in from 203.0.113.77 at 09:41
evidence.why: Proof the password was captured and used: a sign-in from the address that sent the email, 14 minutes after her visit.

evidence.text: SPF, DKIM and DMARC all passed for ashby1ane.example
evidence.why: Explains why the filter let it through, which is the lesson: passing checks proves who sent it, not that they're honest. Useful, but optional here.

evidence.text: whois: ashby1ane.example was registered two days earlier
evidence.why: A brand-new domain is a strong warning sign and worth reporting. It backs up the diagnosis but isn't needed to prove it.

evidence.text: The 'Daniel Ashby' email failed DMARC and went to Junk
evidence.why: A different scam, and the filters caught it. Spoofing the firm's own domain fails DMARC; registering a lookalike doesn't. That contrast is worth knowing, but it isn't how this attacker got in.

evidence.text: Tom's Harlow Print email passed every check
evidence.why: A real email from a real supplier. Telling it apart from the phish is part of triage, but it isn't evidence of the cause.

challenge.debrief: You triaged three reports like a SOC analyst: a real supplier, a spoof the filters caught, and a lookalike that passed every check. You removed it from every mailbox, blocked the domain, and reset the password before ending the sessions so the attacker couldn't walk back in. Real next steps: turn on multi-factor sign-in so a stolen password isn't enough, check Priya's mailbox for new forwarding rules or sent mail, warn Owen and the accounts team, and report the domain to its registrar.
